--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.cmty_edge_btwns()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Detect communities using Edge Betweenness (Girvan-Newman) algorithm. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.cmty_edge_btwns()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Detect communities using Edge Betweenness (Girvan-Newman) algorithm. title: >- [Graph.cmty_edge_btwns()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Detect communities using Edge Betweenness (Girvan-Newman) algorithm. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Detect communities using Edge Betweenness (Girvan-Newman) algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L43347-L43483){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.cmty_edge_btwns( attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Edge-betweenness communities](../assets/graphs/cmty-edge-btwns.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two dense clusters, a triangle A, B, C and a four-node cluster D, E, F, G, joined by the bridge C to D, drawn dashed because every path between the clusters crosses it, so it has the highest betweenness and is the first edge Girvan-Newman cuts. The remaining pieces are the communities: 0 is A, B, C and 1 is D, E, F, G." width="100%"} Iteratively removes edges with highest betweenness centrality to reveal community structure. Uses Brandes' algorithm for efficient betweenness calculation. More accurate than Fast Greedy but significantly slower (`O(m²n)` complexity). Shares its implementation with `cmty_girvan_newman()`, so the two always return the same partition: ties for the highest betweenness go to the edge with the smallest endpoint IDs, and communities are numbered by their smallest node ID. Best for small to medium graphs (< 5K nodes) with hierarchical community structure and clear "bridge" edges between communities. When accuracy is more important than speed. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store community assignments in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `cmty_edge_btwns`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to community IDs (0-indexed, contiguous). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If graph is directed (requires undirected graph). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Girvan-Newman procedure (2002) treats community boundaries as bottlenecks that carry disproportionate edge betweenness: any shortest path connecting two communities must cross one of a few *bridge* edges, so those edges rack up high betweenness scores. The algorithm computes edge betweenness with Brandes' algorithm, removes the current maximum, and repeats, keeping whichever intermediate partition attains the highest modularity. Because betweenness has to be recomputed after every removal, the total cost is $O(m^2 n)$: fine for a few thousand nodes, punishing beyond ten thousand. `cmty_fast_greedy()` and `cmty_louvain()` scale much better, so reach for edge-betweenness when you want the divisive-hierarchical interpretation or when the graph is small enough that the extra cost buys real accuracy. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~cmty_girvan_newman`) : The same algorithm, with any level of the hierarchy and a replay. [](`~edge_betweenness_centrality`) : The edge scores that decide which edge goes next. [](`~modularity`) : The score that picks the level of the hierarchy. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The bridge between these two triangles carries every shortest path from one triangle to the other, so it has by far the highest edge betweenness: ::: {#0ea04bab .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges([ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D"), ]) ( graph.edge_betweenness_centrality() .get_edge_df(labels=True) .select("source", "target", "edge_betweenness_centrality") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### The characters of *Les Misérables* `les_miserables()` links two characters of Victor Hugo's novel when they appear in the same chapter. The busiest edge, from Valjean to Bishop Myriel, is the first to go. Removing edges until modularity peaks leaves 11 communities: ::: {#2ab792bc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl miserables = ec.les_miserables().cmty_edge_btwns() ( miserables.get_node_df() .group_by("cmty_edge_btwns") .agg(pl.len(), pl.col("label")) .sort("cmty_edge_btwns") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

The rest are a few minor characters, alone or in pairs. With 11 communities, the 12 colors of the `"Paired"` palette keep them apart: ::: {#b77944f8 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} miserables.plot( color_by="cmty_edge_btwns", edge_color_by="cmty_edge_btwns", label_by="label", palette="Paired", legend=False, seed=3, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: `cmty_girvan_newman()` runs the same algorithm, and its `n_communities=` returns the other levels of the hierarchy, such as the first split.
